approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would remove or change laws across ten government portfolios to cut red tape for businesses, individuals and community groups.
It would simplify what telecom providers must report, drop duplicate building certification for aged care, and let small-scale importers skip ozone-protection licensing.
The bill also deletes several Acts that are no longer needed, including one that created two construction-industry bodies, one of which was shut down in 1995 and the other has no current members.
Streamlines reporting and information rules for telecom companies under the Competition and Consumer Act 2010.
Removes a certification requirement in the Aged Care Act 1997 that duplicates state, territory and local government building rules.
Exempts low-volume importers from licensing under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989.
Repeals the Act that set up two construction-industry bodies, one abolished in 1995 and the other with no current members.
Repeals the Commonwealth and State Housing Agreement (Service Personnel) Act 1990, which was fully spent after five years.

Businesses, individuals and the community sector affected by regulation in ten portfolios, plus telecommunications providers, aged care providers, low-volume importers, and entities linked to the repealed construction-industry and housing Acts.

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](http://www.openaustralia.org/senate/?id=2014-09-22.180.1) that the bill be read for a third time, which means that the bill is now passed in the Senate. Because the bill has already passed in the House of Representatives, it will now become law. (Read more about the stages that a bill must pass through to become law [here](http://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html). ) _Background to the bill_ The [bill](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/Bills_Search_Results/Result?bId=r5199) was introduced to "reduce regulatory burden for business, individuals and the community sector" (see the [explanatory memorandum](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id%3A%22legislation%2Fems%2Fr5199_ems_904dc708-fca5-4a50-a145-ed1a264af56e%22)) and to repeal redundant provisions that are either duplications or have ceased to have effect. The provisions of the bill that make material changes have been identified and discussed in the [bills digest](http://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1314a/14bd067).

Introduced the Omnibus Repeal Day Bill, saying the previous Labor government added 21,000 new regulations in under six years, including the carbon tax's 18 acts and 1,100 pages of legislation, leaving Australia ranked 128th out of 148 countries for regulatory burden, and said the bill would repeal more than 10,000 acts and regulations, cutting compliance costs by more than $700 million.

Presented a report examining 22 bills and 42 legislative instruments for compatibility with human rights. Raised concerns that national uniform schemes negotiated through COAG can be agreed without formal human rights scrutiny, and sought an update on efforts to address this in drafting protocols for national legislation.

Moved to suspend standing orders to fast-track the Omnibus Repeal Day (Autumn 2014) Bill 2014 and related repeal bills, setting a second reading debate deadline of 5.30 pm and capping the consideration in detail stage at 60 minutes. Said the government intended to pass the bills by the end of the day.

Mocked the substance of the repeal bill, citing examples such as repealing a 1904 Defence Act provision on state naval officers, even though states have had no navies since 1913, and a provision requiring owners to furnish mules and bullocks to the military. Called such repeals irrelevant to business.

Argued the repeal bill's changes were inconsequential, citing a Flags Act 1953 amendment on the size of the Commonwealth Star that had already taken effect, already-spent appropriation acts, and 12 redundant housing assistance acts made obsolete by a later law. Said none of the changes would affect any business.

Noted the Omnibus Repeal Day (Autumn 2014) Bill 2014 repeals or amends 81 pieces of legislation across ten portfolios, and said Labor would support the bill. Flagged plans to move a second reading amendment so government backbenchers would not be embarrassed for straying from the bill's actual content.

Moved a second reading amendment noting Labor's repeal of 16,794 acts, regulations and instruments in government, and that its seamless national economy reforms were estimated to lower business costs by $4 billion a year. Argued most of the bill's changes have no real impact, and accused the government of using it to distract from cuts to protections for ordinary Australians.

Mocked the statute law revision bill as trivial housekeeping dressed up as reform, citing changes such as replacing the hyphenated 'e-mail' with 'email' and fixing a spelling error in the Great Barrier Reef Marine Park Act. Challenged the government to justify its claim that repeal day would save more than $700 million a year by scrapping 9,500 regulations and 1,000 redundant acts.

Supported the Omnibus Repeal Day (Autumn 2014) Bill 2014, arguing excess regulation is hurting productivity, and cited Australia ranking second-last of 51 countries for productivity growth in 2012 and falling to 21st, a slip of six places, in the 2013 Global Competitiveness Index.

Argued the government overstated the Omnibus Repeal Day bill's value, noting the Liberal Party claims it will save business about $700 million a year with communications changes worth only about $35 million of that, and said the Prime Minister's promise of an NBN rollout completed within three years is now broken.

Backed the repeal bill, noting the coalition's target to cut regulatory costs by $1 billion a year and defending the government's technology-agnostic approach to the broadband network rollout, which had passed over 9,000 premises in the past week. Cited the revocation of 46 redundant communications sector instruments as evidence of real deregulation.

Argued the Omnibus Repeal Day bill mostly repeals legislation with no real impact, and criticised the government for abolishing the Australian Charities and Not-for-profits Commission and axing the Commonwealth Cleaning Services Guidelines, which she said will cut between $172 and $225 a week from contract cleaners' pay.

Supported the Omnibus Repeal Day bill's communications measures, noting Telstra currently produces more than 70,000 pages of access agreements for the ACCC each year, and said streamlining reporting requirements would remove more than 1,000 pages of regulation while saving the sector about $35 million a year.

Criticised the government for abolishing the Coordinator-General for Remote Indigenous Services to save $7.1 million over three years, and for withholding $1.1 billion in aged-care workforce supplement funding while claiming credit for building-certification savings the Productivity Commission put at only $350,000 a year.

Supported the repeal bill and pledged $1 billion a year in red tape savings, citing Australia's fall to 21st in the World Economic Forum's Global Competitive Index, a slip of six places in four years, and used a Lego Movie analogy to criticise excessive regulation.
Complimented the member for Parramatta for her detailed contribution highlighting what small businesses face daily, while speaking in support of the Omnibus Repeal Day (Autumn 2014) Bill 2014.

Mocked the government's repeal day rhetoric as grandiose given the changes amount to grammatical corrections like changing 'facsimile' to 'fax', and noted Labor had quietly repealed about 16,000 redundant regulations without launching a website or handbook.

Mocked the Omnibus Repeal Day bill as trivial, citing changes like redefining the size of stars on the Australian flag and replacing facsimile with fax, and argued its real purpose was a smokescreen for unpopular Future of Financial Advice changes worth a claimed $1 billion in savings, ahead of the 5 April WA Senate election.

Supported the Omnibus Repeal Day bill, saying today's repeal of 10,000 regulations would save $700 million, noting Australia ranked 128th out of 148 countries for regulatory burden, and highlighted the Central Coast's 6.88 per cent unemployment rate and 34 per cent youth unemployment rate as reasons deregulation is needed.

Supported the Omnibus Repeal Day bill, which repeals 10,000 pieces and 50,000 pages of legislation saving more than $700 million, contrasted this with the more than 21,000 additional regulations introduced by the previous Labor government, and said more than 10,000 small businesses in her electorate of Macquarie would benefit.

Noted Labor had itself repealed 16,794 redundant acts and regulations in government, delivering $4 billion a year in savings through the Seamless National Economy reforms, and criticised the omnibus bill for hiding a cut that would cost government cleaners between $172 and $255 a week, while the frozen FoFA repeal alone accounted for $200 million of the government's claimed $700 million in savings.

Supported the Omnibus Repeal Day bill, citing an Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry survey finding 44 per cent of businesses spend one to five hours a week on regulatory compliance and 54.3 per cent said it prevented them growing, and said removing duplicate aged-care building certification in the Northern Territory alone would save an estimated $3.42 million.
Complained that the government had gagged debate on the Omnibus Repeal Day bill, calling it an absolute stunt and mocking the coalition's invocation of Ronald Reagan as a model deregulator.
